questions.stem: A seventh-grade teacher is planning a unit that uses live organisms. Which plan is consistent with Florida requirements and accepted practice for K-12 science?
choices: Students perform minor surgery on live frogs under close teacher supervision
Students observe live crayfish behavior, then release them into a nearby canal
Students observe live mealworms and record behavior, using no procedure that harms them
Students expose live mice to a disease so they can compare immune responses
questions.explanation: Florida restricts experiments on live vertebrates in K-12 classrooms: students may not perform surgery or vivisection or subject a live vertebrate to procedures that cause pain, injury, or disease. Non-harmful behavioral observation of invertebrates is appropriate. Releasing classroom organisms outdoors is never acceptable, because it risks introducing a species or a pathogen into the local ecosystem.

questions.stem: A student tells her teacher that she objects to dissecting a preserved specimen. Under Florida requirements, the teacher should
choices: excuse the student and provide an alternative assignment that meets the same objectives
require participation, since the specimen is not a living animal
let the student watch the dissection but record the grade as incomplete
substitute a live-animal activity so the student can still study anatomy
questions.explanation: Florida law allows a student who objects to be excused from performing or observing dissection and provides for an alternative that addresses the same instructional objectives. The idea that objections apply only to living animals is a misreading; the statutory protection covers dissection of preserved specimens as well.

questions.stem: Which practice is correct for storing chemicals in a middle school science storeroom?
choices: Shelve every container alphabetically so items are easy to locate
Store concentrated acids on a high shelf above eye level
Keep flammable liquids beside oxidizers to save cabinet space
Separate chemicals by hazard class and keep corrosives below eye level
questions.explanation: Chemicals must be segregated by compatibility, and corrosives belong in a dedicated cabinet at or below eye level so a leaking container is never lifted past the face. Strict alphabetical storage is the classic mistake, because it can place incompatible neighbors such as an acid next to a cyanide or a flammable next to an oxidizer.

questions.stem: A teacher pours dilute hydrochloric acid from a stock bottle into beakers for six lab groups to use during the period. Which action is required?
choices: Pour any unused acid back into the stock bottle at the end of class
Label each beaker with the chemical identity and hazard information before students use it
Dilute the leftover acid and pour it down the drain without consulting any document
Leave the filled beakers uncovered on the counter until the next class needs them
questions.explanation: Once a chemical is transferred to a container that will be handled by someone other than the person who poured it, that container must carry the identity of the contents and its hazards. Returning unused chemical to the stock bottle is a common shortcut that contaminates the entire supply; leftovers are collected for disposal instead, following the disposal section of the Safety Data Sheet and district rules.

questions.stem: A published activity on chemical weathering calls for concentrated hydrochloric acid. Which substitution best preserves the learning goal while lowering the risk?
choices: Use vinegar on chalk or limestone chips so students can observe and measure the reaction
Show a video of the reaction and cancel the hands-on portion of the lesson
Substitute concentrated sulfuric acid, which is less volatile than hydrochloric acid
Keep the concentrated acid but have students wear gloves while handling it
questions.explanation: A good substitution keeps students investigating the same phenomenon, carbonate rock reacting with acid, using a far less hazardous material. Substituting a different concentrated acid trades one severe hazard for another, and gloves alone do not address splash, spill, or inhalation risk. Replacing the activity with a video preserves safety but gives up the hands-on inquiry that was the point of the lesson.

questions.stem: A teacher needs to know the correct first aid response and the approved disposal method for a chemical in the storeroom. The best source is
choices: the supply company catalog description of the product
the Safety Data Sheet for that specific chemical
the textbook chapter for the lab that uses the chemical
the district purchase order that lists the chemical
questions.explanation: A Safety Data Sheet is organized into 16 standard sections, including first aid measures, handling and storage, exposure controls, and disposal considerations, so it is the authoritative document for both questions. Textbooks and catalogs may give general cautions but are not the required hazard document and may not match the specific concentration on the shelf.

questions.stem: Under the OSHA Hazard Communication Standard, an employer that keeps hazardous chemicals on site must
choices: keep all Safety Data Sheets locked in the administrative office
maintain Safety Data Sheets only for chemicals purchased within the past year
maintain Safety Data Sheets that employees can reach during their work shift and train employees on chemical hazards
mail copies of all Safety Data Sheets to the state each August
questions.explanation: The standard requires a written hazard communication program, labels on containers, Safety Data Sheets that are readily accessible to employees during each work shift, and employee training on the hazards present. Locking the sheets in an office defeats the purpose, since the information is needed immediately at the moment of a spill or exposure.

questions.stem: A lab where students work with dilute sodium hydroxide must have an emergency eyewash station that
choices: is kept in a locked cabinet and issued by the teacher when needed
delivers a brief high-pressure spray to clear the eye quickly
may be anywhere in the building as long as the staff know its location
is unobstructed, reachable in about ten seconds, and can flush both eyes for 15 minutes
questions.explanation: The widely adopted consensus standard calls for an eyewash on an unobstructed path within roughly ten seconds of travel from the hazard, supplying a gentle flow of tepid water to both eyes for a full 15 minutes. A high-pressure spray is unsafe, because it can drive contaminants deeper and injure the eye, and any station that must be unlocked or fetched is not available fast enough.

questions.stem: Students will heat solutions on hot plates and mix dilute acids in a middle school lab. What eye protection is appropriate?
choices: Chemical splash goggles that seal around the eyes, worn by students, the teacher, and any visitors
Safety glasses with side shields, which are sufficient protection against any liquid
Ordinary prescription eyeglasses, since the lenses already cover the eyes
Eye protection is optional whenever the solutions used are dilute
questions.explanation: Florida requires that industrial-quality eye-protective devices be furnished and worn in school laboratories and shops where caustic or explosive chemicals, hot liquids or solids, or flying particles create a risk of eye injury, and the requirement covers teachers and visitors in the room as well as students. Safety glasses are rated for impact, not splash: liquid can enter around the frame, so sealed splash goggles are the correct choice here.

questions.stem: Before beginning a unit on the seasons, a teacher asks each student to draw and label why summer is warmer than winter, then reads all the responses that night. This assessment is best described as
choices: a summative assessment of the seasons unit
an accommodation for students who struggle with reading
a diagnostic formative assessment used to surface misconceptions before instruction
a performance task designed to produce a grade for the modeling practice
questions.explanation: The purpose is to find out what students already think so instruction can be adjusted, which is the defining feature of formative assessment, and giving it before instruction makes it diagnostic. Students and teachers often equate any written task with summative assessment, but summative assessment is given at the end of instruction to judge how much was learned.

questions.stem: Most students in a class believe a heavier ball must fall faster than a lighter one. Which instructional response is most likely to change that belief?
choices: Stating the correct rule clearly and having students copy it three times
Assigning a reading that says all objects fall at the same rate
Giving a quiz on the value of the acceleration due to gravity
Having students commit to a prediction, drop the objects, then reconcile the result with what they predicted
questions.explanation: Misconceptions are resistant to being told the right answer; students need to make their thinking explicit, meet evidence that contradicts it, and then rebuild the explanation, which is the logic of a predict, observe, explain sequence. Restating or rereading the correct rule usually produces students who can recite the rule while keeping the original belief intact.

questions.stem: A teacher gives students the question 'How does ramp angle affect how far a toy car rolls?' plus a bin of materials, and each group designs its own procedure. This activity is best classified as
choices: confirmation inquiry
guided inquiry
open inquiry
structured inquiry
questions.explanation: In guided inquiry the teacher supplies the question and materials while students design the procedure and determine the results. Structured inquiry is the frequent mix-up: there the teacher supplies the procedure too. In open inquiry students generate the question themselves, and in confirmation inquiry the outcome is already known and students verify it.

questions.stem: Students need to see how temperature changes second by second during a fast exothermic reaction. Which technology best supports that goal?
choices: A class set of tablets used to watch a recorded demonstration of the reaction
A word processor for writing up the conclusion after the lab
A temperature probe linked to a data collection device that graphs readings in real time
A presentation program for sharing the group results with the class
questions.explanation: Probeware samples far faster than a student reading a thermometer and displays the graph as the reaction happens, so students can connect the shape of the curve to what they observe. The other tools are useful for other purposes, and choosing them here reflects the common error of selecting technology for engagement rather than for the specific learning goal.

questions.stem: A student records the following about an insect in a terrarium. Which statement is an inference rather than an observation?
choices: The insect has six legs and two antennae
The insect is 12 mm long
The insect is searching for food
The insect moved 4 cm in 30 seconds
questions.explanation: An observation is information gathered directly through the senses or an instrument, while an inference is an interpretation of what those observations mean. Saying the insect is searching for food adds a purpose that was never observed. Students often treat a confident, reasonable interpretation as an observation, but reasonableness is not the test.

questions.stem: Which of these is a quantitative observation of a chemical reaction?
choices: The mixture gives off a sharp odor
The temperature of the mixture rises by 8.5 degrees Celsius
The solution changes from clear to cloudy
Bubbles form on the surface of the metal
questions.explanation: Quantitative observations record an amount using a number and a unit, while qualitative observations describe a quality such as color, odor, or texture. Students sometimes count the bubbles description as quantitative because bubbles could be counted, but as written it reports no measurement.

questions.stem: A block has a known mass of 50.0 g. A student weighs it four times and gets 47.1, 47.2, 47.1, and 47.2 g. These results are best described as
choices: accurate but not precise
both accurate and precise
neither accurate nor precise
precise but not accurate
questions.explanation: Precision is how closely repeated measurements agree with one another, and these four agree within 0.1 g. Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value, and every reading is about 3 g low, which points to a balance that needs to be zeroed or calibrated. Treating the two words as synonyms is the misconception this item targets.

questions.stem: A student finishes an investigation on how light color affects plant growth. Which product best communicates her findings to a scientific audience?
choices: A poster that shows only her original hypothesis and her conclusion
A report with her procedure, a data table and graph, and a conclusion that cites the data
A written story describing what she had hoped would happen in the experiment
A slideshow of photographs of the plants taken on the final day
questions.explanation: Scientific communication has to let others evaluate and repeat the work, which requires the procedure, the actual data, and reasoning that connects the evidence to the claim. A conclusion presented without the supporting data cannot be checked by anyone else, and photographs alone document appearance without the measurements that were collected.

questions.stem: To test whether fertilizer amount affects tomato plant height, a student grows plants that receive 0, 5, 10, or 20 mL of fertilizer solution per week and measures each plant's height after 30 days. The independent variable is
choices: the height of each plant after 30 days
the amount of fertilizer solution given each week
the 30-day length of the investigation
the type of potting soil used in every pot
questions.explanation: The independent variable is the one factor the investigator deliberately changes between groups, which here is the volume of fertilizer solution. Plant height is what responds and is measured, so it is the dependent variable, and the soil type is deliberately held the same, making it a constant. Reversing the independent and dependent variables is the single most common error on items like this.

questions.stem: To test whether fertilizer amount affects tomato plant height, a student grows plants that receive 0, 5, 10, or 20 mL of fertilizer solution per week and measures each plant's height after 30 days. In this investigation, the dependent variable is
choices: plant height measured after 30 days
the amount of fertilizer solution given
the amount of sunlight each plant receives
the size of the pot each plant grows in
questions.explanation: The dependent variable is what the investigator measures to see whether it responds to the change, and here that is plant height. A useful memory hook is that the dependent variable depends on the independent variable. Sunlight and pot size are held constant, so they are controlled variables rather than the measured outcome.

questions.stem: To test whether fertilizer amount affects tomato plant height, a student grows plants that receive 0, 5, 10, or 20 mL of fertilizer solution per week and measures each plant's height after 30 days. Which group serves as the control group?
choices: The plants that receive 20 mL of fertilizer solution per week
The plants that receive 10 mL of fertilizer solution per week
The plants that receive 0 mL of fertilizer solution per week
All of the plants together, since they share identical soil
questions.explanation: The control group receives no treatment and provides the baseline that the treated groups are compared against, so here it is the plants given no fertilizer. Students often confuse the control group with the controlled variables; the control group is a group of subjects, while controlled variables are the conditions held the same for everyone.

questions.stem: To test whether fertilizer amount affects tomato plant height, a student grows plants that receive 0, 5, 10, or 20 mL of fertilizer solution per week and measures each plant's height after 30 days. Which factor must be kept the same for every group?
choices: The volume of fertilizer solution added each week
The final height reached by each plant
The number of leaves each plant produces
The water, light, and soil type each plant receives
questions.explanation: Controlled variables, also called constants, are the conditions deliberately held identical so any difference in the outcome can be attributed to the independent variable. Fertilizer volume is the one thing that must differ, and plant height and leaf count are outcomes that are measured, not controlled. Listing an outcome as a constant is a frequent error.

questions.stem: A student asks whether container color affects how fast water warms in sunlight. She fills four identical bottles with 250 mL of water, paints them white, yellow, red, and black, sets all four in the same sunny spot, and records temperature every 10 minutes for an hour. Which statement about her design is accurate?
choices: The independent variable is time and the dependent variable is bottle color
The design is invalid because she has no control group at all
Bottle color is the independent variable, temperature is the dependent variable, and volume, bottle size, and location are constants
She has four independent variables because she used four different bottles
questions.explanation: The one factor she changed on purpose is the paint color, the thing she measured in response is water temperature, and everything else was deliberately matched so it stayed constant. The four bottles are four levels of a single independent variable, not four separate variables, which is a very common misreading. The white bottle serves as a reasonable comparison baseline even though no group is left unpainted.

questions.stem: A student tests a plant food. She puts the treated plant on a sunny windowsill and waters it daily; she puts the untreated plant in a hallway and waters it weekly. The treated plant grows more, and she concludes the plant food works. What is the main problem?
choices: Her hypothesis should have been written in the form of a question
More than one condition differed between the plants, so the cause of the difference cannot be identified
She would need to run the investigation for a full year before drawing any conclusion
Plant height cannot serve as a dependent variable because it changes continuously
questions.explanation: Light and watering frequency both differed along with the plant food, so those variables are confounded and no single cause can be assigned to the growth difference. Students often focus on trial length or sample size, which do matter, but the fatal flaw here is failing to hold the other conditions constant.

questions.stem: Which measurement is reported in an SI base unit?
choices: A mass of 2.5 kilograms
A volume of 500 milliliters
A temperature of 25 degrees Celsius
A speed of 12 meters per second
questions.explanation: The kilogram is the SI base unit of mass, one of the seven base units along with the meter, second, kelvin, mole, ampere, and candela. The liter is a widely used metric unit but not an SI base unit, the SI base unit of temperature is the kelvin rather than the degree Celsius, and meters per second is a derived unit built from two base units.

questions.stem: How many micrometers are there in one millimeter?
questions.explanation: Milli means one thousandth and micro means one millionth, so a millimeter is a thousand times larger than a micrometer. Choosing one million is the usual slip: that is how many micrometers fit in a meter, not in a millimeter.

questions.stem: A student reports that a cell is 45 micrometers across. Expressed in meters, that length is
questions.explanation: One micrometer equals 10^-6 m, so 45 micrometers equals 45 x 10^-6 m, which is written in proper scientific notation as 4.5 x 10^-5 m. A frequent error is writing 4.5 x 10^-6 or 45 x 10^-6 without adjusting the exponent after moving the decimal point one place to the left.

questions.stem: A student measures a block's mass as 12.5 g and its volume as 4.0 mL. Reported with the correct number of significant figures, the density is
choices: 3.1 g/mL
3 g/mL
questions.explanation: The calculator gives 3.125, but in multiplication and division the answer carries the number of significant figures of the least precise measurement, and 4.0 mL has only two. Reporting all four digits from the calculator display is the standard mistake, because it claims more precision than the measuring tools actually delivered.

questions.stem: Five trials of a reaction time test give 0.22, 0.25, 0.24, 0.23, and 0.95 seconds. Which statement about these data is best supported?
choices: The mean is the best measure of center here because it uses every value
The range is 0.03 s, which shows the data are tightly clustered
The median of 0.24 s represents typical performance better, because one outlier pulls the mean upward
The 0.95 s trial should simply be deleted so the summary looks cleaner
questions.explanation: The mean of these values is about 0.38 s, higher than four of the five trials, because the single 0.95 s outlier drags it upward, while the median of 0.24 s sits among the typical values. The range is the largest value minus the smallest, or 0.73 s, not 0.03 s. Outliers are investigated and reported, not quietly deleted.

questions.stem: A student records the temperature of a cooling beaker of water every two minutes for 30 minutes. Which display best shows these data?
choices: A circle graph showing each temperature reading as a share of the whole
A bar graph with a separate bar for each two-minute reading
A histogram grouping the temperatures into intervals
A line graph with time on the x-axis and temperature on the y-axis
questions.explanation: A line graph is the right choice when both variables are continuous and the point is to show how one changes over time, and by convention the independent variable goes on the x-axis. Bar graphs compare separate categories, and a circle graph shows parts of a whole, which is meaningless for temperature readings that do not sum to anything.

questions.stem: An astronomer studies how stars of different masses age. She cannot manipulate a star, so she compares thousands of stars at different stages of their life cycles. Her approach is
choices: scientific, because systematic observation and comparison can test predictions even without manipulation
not scientific, because she never performs a controlled experiment
scientific only if she also builds a working laboratory model of a star
not scientific, because no one else could ever repeat her work
questions.explanation: Controlled experimentation is one method in science, not the definition of science; astronomy, geology, and paleontology test hypotheses by predicting what patterns should appear in observations and then checking. The idea that nothing counts as science without a lab experiment is a widespread misconception, and observational studies are repeatable because other astronomers can examine the same objects and data.

questions.stem: Which question is best investigated through a controlled experiment rather than by observation alone?
choices: How has the shoreline of a barrier island shifted over the past 50 years?
Which kinds of fossils occur in a particular limestone layer?
Does adding phosphate to pond water increase algae growth?
Which stars in a constellation appear brightest from Earth?
questions.explanation: Only the phosphate question involves a variable an investigator can deliberately manipulate while holding other conditions constant, which is what a controlled experiment requires. The other three ask about conditions that already exist or events that already happened, so they are answered by careful measurement and comparison rather than by treatment groups.

questions.stem: A geologist and a chemist both investigate how limestone dissolves. Which statement best compares their methods?
choices: Only the chemist is doing science, because only she runs experiments
Only the geologist is doing science, because only he studies the real world
Their methods are identical, since every science follows one fixed sequence of steps
Both use evidence and logic, but the chemist controls lab conditions while the geologist relies more on field observation
questions.explanation: Different fields share the commitment to evidence, reasoning, and openness to review, but they differ in how much of the system can be manipulated and over what timescale. The idea of a single fixed scientific method performed in the same order by everyone is a textbook simplification that does not describe how scientists actually work.

questions.stem: A researcher's data do not support the hypothesis she expected to confirm. Which response best reflects the habits of a scientist?
choices: Report the results accurately and consider what the evidence actually shows
Repeat the study until the expected result appears, then publish only that trial
Adjust a few data points so the pattern comes out clearer
Set the study aside, since results that fail to confirm a hypothesis have no value
questions.explanation: Honesty about data, including data that contradict expectations, is fundamental, and disconfirming results often lead to the most important revisions in understanding. Selecting only the run that matched the expectation is cherry-picking, and it produces conclusions that other researchers will fail to reproduce.

questions.stem: Peer review strengthens scientific knowledge mainly because it
choices: guarantees that everything published in a journal is correct
lets other qualified scientists examine the methods, reasoning, and evidence before publication
ensures that only widely accepted ideas make it into print
measures how popular a particular research topic has become
questions.explanation: Peer review is a quality check in which independent experts look for flaws in design, analysis, and interpretation before a study reaches the wider community. It reduces error but does not guarantee truth, since reviewed papers are sometimes later overturned; treating peer review as a guarantee that everything published is correct is the misconception behind that distractor.

questions.stem: Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in the early 1900s, but most geologists rejected it until seafloor evidence in the 1960s supported plate tectonics. This history best illustrates that scientific knowledge is
choices: unreliable, since experts were wrong for several decades
settled by majority opinion rather than by evidence
permanent once a respected scientist has proposed an idea
durable but open to revision when new evidence is strong enough
questions.explanation: Wegener lacked a mechanism, and the community changed its mind only when seafloor spreading and magnetic striping supplied one, which is exactly how science is supposed to work. Concluding that science is therefore unreliable is a common overcorrection; self-correction in response to evidence is a strength, not a defect.

questions.stem: Which assumption underlies all scientific investigation?
choices: Natural events have natural causes that follow consistent patterns
Every scientific question has one final answer that will never change
Only work done inside a laboratory can produce valid evidence
A claim is true when a recognized authority in the field states it
questions.explanation: Science assumes the universe is orderly and comprehensible, so that patterns observed today will hold tomorrow and elsewhere, which is what makes prediction and replication possible. The appeal to authority, calling a claim true because a recognized expert states it, is the opposite of scientific practice, where a claim from any source must still survive testing against evidence.

questions.stem: Which question cannot be answered by scientific investigation?
choices: Does caffeine change the resting heart rate of adults?
Is it morally right to keep dolphins in aquariums?
How does soil pH affect blueberry yield?
Which gases make up the atmosphere of Mars?
questions.explanation: Science can gather evidence about dolphin health, stress, and behavior in captivity, but whether keeping them is morally right is a value judgment that no measurement can settle. Students sometimes assume any question involving a scientific topic is a scientific question; the test is whether evidence could in principle decide the answer.

questions.stem: A student proposes to investigate 'Which butterfly species is the most beautiful?' The teacher should explain that this question
choices: cannot be settled with evidence because beauty is a preference, and help her write a measurable question instead
is fine as written, because the class can vote and use the winner as the answer
becomes testable if she surveys enough people, since the majority answer would be the correct one
should be replaced with a question about how the universe began
questions.explanation: Beauty is a matter of taste, so no observation could show one species is objectively most beautiful; a measurable version might ask which species most visitors report noticing first, or which wing colors attract the most pollinator visits. The survey distractor is subtle: a survey can accurately measure what people prefer, but popularity does not establish a fact about the butterflies themselves.

questions.stem: The development of the compound microscope in the 1600s contributed most directly to
choices: acceptance of the geocentric model of the solar system
the statement of the law of conservation of mass
the discovery of cells and, much later, the germ theory of disease
the organization of the elements into the periodic table
questions.explanation: New instruments open new domains of observation, and the microscope revealed cells and microorganisms that no one could previously see, which eventually made germ theory possible. This illustrates that advances in technology and advances in scientific knowledge drive each other rather than one simply applying the other.

questions.stem: Which statement about the cultural development of science is accurate?
choices: Modern science arose in a single culture with no contributions from elsewhere
Knowledge from earlier cultures was discarded rather than built upon
Only European scholars contributed to early astronomy and mathematics
Scholars in many cultures, including the medieval Islamic world, China, and India, produced work that later science built upon
questions.explanation: Astronomy, mathematics, optics, medicine, and metallurgy all developed across many societies, and ideas moved between them through trade, translation, and travel. The view that science began in one place and moved outward is a persistent misconception that erases the record of earlier observations and methods that later scientists depended on.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a scientific law from a scientific theory?
choices: A law describes a consistent relationship in nature; a theory explains why that relationship occurs
A law is a theory that has been proven true beyond any possible doubt
A theory is a guess, while a law is the version supported by evidence
A theory turns into a law once enough experiments have confirmed it
questions.explanation: Laws describe and often quantify what reliably happens, such as the law of universal gravitation, while theories are broad explanations of why, such as general relativity. The idea that a theory graduates into a law after enough testing is the most common misconception in this topic; they are different kinds of knowledge, and neither ranks above the other.

questions.stem: Which statement is a scientific hypothesis?
choices: Plants are the most important organisms on Earth
If seedlings are grown under blue light, they will grow taller than seedlings under red light
Why do seedlings bend toward a window?
Life could not exist anywhere without light
questions.explanation: A hypothesis is a proposed, testable explanation or prediction that could be shown to be wrong by evidence, and the blue and red light statement can be checked by measuring seedlings. The statement about seedlings bending toward a window is a question rather than a hypothesis, and the claim that plants are the most important organisms is a value judgment that no measurement can settle.

questions.stem: A student says, 'Evolution is only a theory, so it has not really been established.' The best correction is that in science a theory
choices: is an idea that has been partly tested but is not yet accepted by scientists
must be converted into a law before it counts as reliable knowledge
is a broad, well-supported explanation backed by many independent lines of evidence
is the same thing as a hypothesis, only stated in more formal language
questions.explanation: The everyday meaning of theory, a hunch or guess, is nearly the opposite of the scientific meaning, which requires extensive testing and convergent evidence from independent sources. Equating a theory with a hypothesis is the underlying error; a hypothesis is a single testable proposal, while a theory organizes and explains a large body of confirmed findings.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a ball-and-stick model of a water molecule. What is the most important limitation for students to understand?
choices: The model shows the wrong number of atoms in a water molecule
Models are opinions, so they cannot be used as evidence at all
The model cannot be used to predict anything about how water behaves
The model simplifies reality: atoms are not solid colored balls and bonds are not rigid sticks
questions.explanation: Every model highlights some features and distorts or omits others, so knowing what a model leaves out is part of using it well; this one shows connectivity and shape but misrepresents scale, motion, and the nature of bonding. Concluding that models are therefore useless is the overcorrection in the option calling models mere opinions and the one denying any predictive value, since this model still predicts the bent geometry that explains water's polarity.

questions.stem: A county is deciding whether to restrict fertilizer use near a bay where algal blooms are worsening. Which statement best describes the role of science in that decision?
choices: Science can describe the link between nutrient loading and blooms and predict outcomes, but the decision also weighs economic and social values
Science alone determines the correct policy, so the data should decide the rule automatically
Science has no role, because the issue involves money and politics rather than facts
Scientists should write the ordinance themselves, since they understand the evidence best
questions.explanation: Scientific evidence can establish what is happening and forecast what different actions would produce, but choosing among options requires judgments about cost, fairness, and priorities that evidence alone cannot supply. The belief that data automatically dictate policy overlooks the value trade-offs at the heart of most environmental decisions.

questions.stem: Funding for research on a particular disease rises sharply after a large public awareness campaign. This best illustrates that
choices: scientific conclusions are determined by public opinion
science can advance only when the general public understands it
social and political priorities influence which scientific questions get investigated
the methods of science change to match the interests of funding sources
questions.explanation: Society shapes the agenda of science by directing money and attention toward some problems rather than others, which affects what gets studied and how quickly. What society does not determine is the answer: the data still decide whether a treatment works, so the claim that public opinion sets scientific conclusions confuses agenda with evidence.

cards.front: Write the formula for density, and say what each symbol stands for.
cards.back: Density = mass / volume (D = m/V), usually in g/cm³ or g/mL. Water's density is 1.0 g/cm³, the benchmark for floating and sinking.

cards.front: How do you predict whether an object will float or sink in a liquid?
cards.back: Compare densities: an object floats if its density is less than the liquid's and sinks if it is greater. A huge steel ship floats because its overall density (steel plus air inside) is below 1.0 g/cm³.

cards.front: What is the difference between mass and weight?
cards.back: Mass is the amount of matter, measured in kg, and is the same everywhere. Weight is the force of gravity on that mass, W = mg, measured in newtons; a 10 kg rock weighs 98 N on Earth but only about 16 N on the Moon.

cards.front: How can you tell a physical change from a chemical change?
cards.back: A physical change alters form or state but not identity (melting ice, dissolving sugar, tearing paper). A chemical change produces a new substance with different properties (rusting, burning, tarnishing).

cards.front: Name four observations that signal a chemical change has occurred.
cards.back: Gas production (bubbles without boiling), a precipitate forming, an unexpected color change, and energy release or absorption (heat, light). Any one suggests a new substance formed.

cards.front: Describe particle arrangement and motion in solids, liquids, and gases.
cards.back: Solid: particles packed in fixed positions, vibrating in place (definite shape and volume). Liquid: particles close but able to slide past each other (definite volume, takes container's shape). Gas: particles far apart, moving fast and freely (fills its container).

cards.front: What is plasma and where do you encounter it?
cards.back: Plasma is a superheated, ionized gas in which electrons have been stripped from atoms, so it conducts electricity. It is the most common state of matter in the universe: stars, lightning, and neon signs.

cards.front: What are sublimation and deposition? Give an example of each.
cards.back: Sublimation is solid changing directly to gas, like dry ice shrinking with no puddle. Deposition is gas changing directly to solid, like frost forming on a cold window.

cards.front: Why does temperature stay constant while a substance melts or boils?
cards.back: The added energy goes into overcoming attractions between particles (raising potential energy) instead of speeding the particles up. Only after the phase change finishes does temperature rise again; a heating curve is flat during each phase change.

cards.front: Write the equation for converting degrees Celsius to Kelvin.
cards.back: K = °C + 273. Kelvin starts at absolute zero, so it is directly proportional to average particle kinetic energy; Celsius ratios give wrong answers because 0°C is not zero energy.

cards.front: Write the equation for Boyle's law.
cards.back: At constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely related: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂. Squeeze a sealed syringe to half its volume and the pressure doubles.

cards.front: Write the equation for Charles's law.
cards.back: At constant pressure, volume is directly proportional to Kelvin temperature: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂. A balloon expands in a hot car and shrinks in a freezer.

cards.front: Write the equation for Gay-Lussac's law.
cards.back: At constant volume, pressure is directly proportional to Kelvin temperature: P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂. This is why a rigid aerosol can may burst if heated in a fire.

cards.front: Write the ideal gas law equation.
cards.back: PV = nRT: pressure x volume = moles x gas constant x Kelvin temperature. It combines Boyle's, Charles's, and Avogadro's relationships into one equation.

cards.front: According to kinetic molecular theory, what causes gas pressure?
cards.back: Countless collisions of fast-moving gas particles against the container walls. More particles, a smaller container, or higher temperature all mean more or harder collisions, so pressure rises.

cards.front: What did John Dalton contribute to atomic theory?
cards.back: Dalton (early 1800s) proposed that all matter is made of indivisible atoms, that atoms of one element are identical, and that atoms combine in whole-number ratios to form compounds. Later discoveries of subatomic particles and isotopes revised the first two points. Hook: Dalton is the starting dot, a plain solid ball with nothing inside. No particle, no apparatus, just: atoms exist.

cards.front: What did J.J. Thomson discover, with what apparatus, and what model did he propose?
cards.back: Using cathode ray tubes (1897), Thomson discovered the electron, proving atoms contain smaller particles. He proposed the plum pudding model: negative electrons embedded in a sphere of positive charge. Hook: Thomson found something smaller THan the atom. Cathode ray tube leads to electron leads to plum pudding.

cards.front: What did Rutherford's gold foil experiment show?
cards.back: Most alpha particles passed through the foil but a few bounced back, so the atom is mostly empty space with a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus. This overthrew the plum pudding model. Hook: Rutherford is the nucleus man. Gold foil leads to core. Bounce-back means dense positive center; pass-through means empty space.

cards.front: What did Niels Bohr add to the model of the atom?
cards.back: Bohr (1913) proposed that electrons occupy specific, fixed energy levels and jump between them by absorbing or emitting exact amounts of light. This explained the line spectra of elements. Hook: Bohr = floors. Electrons stand on fixed floors and jump between them, never in between; each jump is one exact color of light.

cards.front: What did James Chadwick discover, and what did it explain?
cards.back: Chadwick discovered the neutron (1932), a neutral particle in the nucleus. Neutrons explain why isotopes of an element differ in mass while behaving identically in chemical reactions. Hook: Chadwick closes the story with the neutral one. Neutron adds mass without charge, which is exactly what makes isotopes.

cards.front: How did Schrodinger change the picture of the electron?
cards.back: Schrodinger's quantum model (1926) replaced fixed orbits with orbitals: cloud-like regions describing where an electron is likely to be found. This probability-based electron cloud model is the modern view. Hook: Schrodinger is the cloud of maybe, like his cat: probabilities, not positions.

cards.front: Put the six atomic-theory scientists in date order and give each one's single key contribution.
cards.back: Dalton's Theory Really Bothered Some Chemists: Dalton 1803 (solid ball, atoms are real), Thomson 1897 (cathode rays, ELECTRON, plum pudding), Rutherford 1911 (gold foil, NUCLEUS, empty space), Bohr 1913 (fixed energy levels, line spectra), Schrodinger 1926 (electron CLOUD, probability), Chadwick 1932 (NEUTRON, explains isotopes). Only Thomson, Rutherford, and Chadwick found particles; the rest changed the model.

cards.front: Give the charge, approximate mass, and location of the proton, neutron, and electron.
cards.back: Proton: +1 charge, mass about 1 amu, in the nucleus. Neutron: no charge, about 1 amu, in the nucleus. Electron: -1 charge, about 1/1836 amu (nearly negligible), outside the nucleus in energy levels.

cards.front: Write the rule for finding the number of neutrons in an atom from its mass number and atomic number.
cards.back: Atomic number = number of protons, which defines the element. Mass number = protons + neutrons. Neutrons = mass number - atomic number; for sodium-23 (Z = 11), that is 23 - 11 = 12.

cards.front: What makes two atoms isotopes of the same element?
cards.back: Same number of protons, different number of neutrons, so same chemical behavior but different mass. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have 6 protons, but 6 and 8 neutrons respectively.

cards.front: What happens when an atom loses electrons? Gains electrons?
cards.back: Losing electrons leaves excess protons, making a positive ion (cation), like Na⁺ or Ca²⁺; metals do this. Gaining electrons makes a negative ion (anion), like Cl⁻; nonmetals do this. Proton count never changes.

cards.front: Distinguish an element, a compound, and a mixture.
cards.back: Element: one kind of atom (O₂, gold). Compound: two or more elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio (H₂O, NaCl). Mixture: substances physically combined in variable proportions, separable by physical means (salt water, air).

cards.front: What is the difference between a homogeneous and a heterogeneous mixture?
cards.back: A homogeneous mixture is uniform throughout, like salt water or air; you cannot see the parts. A heterogeneous mixture has visibly distinct parts, like trail mix or muddy water.

cards.front: Match the separation method to the mixture: dissolved salt, sand in water, iron filings in sand, ink pigments.
cards.back: Dissolved salt: evaporation or distillation. Sand in water: filtration. Iron filings: magnet. Ink pigments: chromatography. All are physical methods, which is what proves these are mixtures, not compounds.

cards.front: Write the chemical formulas for water, carbon dioxide, table salt, methane, and ammonia, in that order.
cards.back: Water H₂O, carbon dioxide CO₂, table salt NaCl, methane CH₄, ammonia NH₃. Methane is the simplest organic (carbon-based) compound of the five.

cards.front: What defines an acid? Give its pH range, indicator behavior, and two examples.
cards.back: An acid releases hydrogen ions (H⁺) in water; pH below 7; turns blue litmus red; tastes sour. Examples: hydrochloric acid HCl (stomach acid) and sulfuric acid H₂SO₄ (car batteries).

cards.front: What defines a base? Give its pH range, indicator behavior, and two examples.
cards.back: A base releases hydroxide ions (OH⁻) in water or accepts H⁺; pH above 7; turns red litmus blue; feels slippery. Examples: sodium hydroxide NaOH (drain cleaner) and ammonia NH₃.

cards.front: What does a change of one pH unit represent?
cards.back: A tenfold (10x) change in hydrogen ion concentration, because the scale is logarithmic. pH 4 is 10 times more acidic than pH 5 and 100 times more acidic than pH 6; pH 7 is neutral.

cards.front: What are the products when an acid reacts with a base? Give an example equation.
cards.back: A salt plus water. Example: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. The H⁺ and OH⁻ combine into water, and the leftover ions form the salt.

cards.front: Why must chemical equations be balanced, and what may you change to balance them?
cards.back: The law of conservation of mass: atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a reaction, so each element needs equal counts on both sides. Adjust only the coefficients in front of formulas, never the subscripts, which would change the substances.

cards.front: On the periodic table, what do a group and a period tell you about an element?
cards.back: A group (vertical column) shares the same number of valence electrons, so members have similar chemical properties. A period (horizontal row) tells you how many occupied energy levels the atom has.

cards.front: Describe the alkali metals, halogens, and noble gases.
cards.back: Alkali metals (Group 1): soft, extremely reactive metals with 1 valence electron (Na, K). Halogens (Group 17): reactive nonmetals with 7 valence electrons that form salts (Cl, F). Noble gases (Group 18): full valence shells, almost completely unreactive (He, Ne, Ar).

cards.front: How does reactivity change moving down Group 1 (metals) versus down Group 17 (halogens)?
cards.back: Metal reactivity increases down the group (cesium is more reactive than lithium) because the valence electron is farther out and easier to lose. Halogen reactivity decreases down the group; fluorine at the top is the most reactive because it gains an electron most easily.

cards.front: What happens in ionic bonding, and what properties do ionic compounds have?
cards.back: A metal transfers electrons to a nonmetal, and the resulting oppositely charged ions attract, as in NaCl. Ionic compounds form brittle crystals with high melting points and conduct electricity when molten or dissolved, not as solids.

cards.front: What happens in covalent bonding, and what properties do covalent compounds tend to have?
cards.back: Two nonmetals share pairs of electrons to form molecules, as in H₂O and CO₂. Molecular compounds generally have lower melting and boiling points and do not conduct electricity.

cards.front: What is the sea of electrons model, and which metal properties does it explain?
cards.back: In metals, valence electrons detach and move freely among a lattice of positive ions. The mobile electrons explain electrical and thermal conductivity, and the non-directional bonding explains malleability and ductility.

cards.front: What is a hydrogen bond, and what does it explain about water?
cards.back: An attraction between a hydrogen atom in one molecule and an electronegative atom (O, N, F) in a neighboring molecule; it is intermolecular, weaker than a covalent bond. Hydrogen bonds give water its high boiling point, strong surface tension, and ice that floats.

cards.front: Give the general patterns for synthesis, decomposition, single replacement, double replacement, and combustion reactions.
cards.back: Synthesis: A + B → AB. Decomposition: AB → A + B. Single replacement: A + BC → AC + B. Double replacement: AB + CD → AD + CB. Combustion: fuel + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O, releasing energy.

cards.front: Write the formula for average speed.
cards.back: v = d/t, distance divided by time, in m/s or km/h. Example: 150 km in 2.5 h is 150/2.5 = 60 km/h.

cards.front: Write the formula for acceleration.
cards.back: a = Δv/t, the change in velocity divided by the time it takes, in m/s². Going from 0 to 24 m/s in 6 s is an acceleration of 4 m/s².

cards.front: Write the equation relating net force, mass, and acceleration.
cards.back: F = ma (net force = mass x acceleration). One newton is the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s², so 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².

cards.front: Write the formula for the weight of an object.
cards.back: W = mg, with g = 9.8 m/s² on Earth's surface. A 10 kg object weighs 98 N; weight is a force in newtons, not kilograms.

cards.front: Write the formula for linear momentum.
cards.back: p = mv, mass times velocity, in kg·m/s. A 1,200 kg car at 5 m/s has 6,000 kg·m/s of momentum; both mass and velocity matter equally.

cards.front: What is the difference between speed and velocity?
cards.back: Speed is how fast (magnitude only); velocity is speed plus direction. A car circling a track at a steady 60 km/h has constant speed but constantly changing velocity because its direction changes.

cards.front: Name three ways an object can accelerate.
cards.back: Speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction; acceleration is any change in velocity. A turning car accelerates even at constant speed, and braking is acceleration opposite the motion.

cards.front: State Newton's first law and give an everyday example.
cards.back: An object stays at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless acted on by a net external force (the law of inertia). Example: passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes because their bodies keep moving; seat belts supply the stopping force.

cards.front: State Newton's second law in words.
cards.back: Acceleration is directly proportional to the net force and inversely proportional to the mass: a = F/m. Doubling the force doubles the acceleration; doubling the mass halves it.

cards.front: State Newton's third law, and explain why the paired forces never cancel.
cards.back: For every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force. The two forces act on different objects (foot pushes ground, ground pushes foot), so neither object's net force is automatically zero.

cards.front: What is the difference between balanced and unbalanced forces?
cards.back: Balanced forces sum to zero net force: the object's motion does not change (rest or constant velocity). Unbalanced forces produce a nonzero net force and therefore an acceleration in the direction of that net force.

cards.front: What is friction, and which direction does it act?
cards.back: Friction is a contact force that opposes sliding or attempted sliding between surfaces. Static friction holds stationary objects in place; kinetic friction acts on moving objects, converting kinetic energy to heat.

cards.front: Sort these into contact forces and forces at a distance: friction, gravity, tension, magnetism, normal force, electric force.
cards.back: Contact: friction, tension, normal force (require touching). At a distance (field forces): gravity, magnetism, electric force; they act through fields and need no contact.

cards.front: How does gravitational force depend on mass and on distance?
cards.back: It increases with the product of the two masses and decreases with the square of the distance between them (inverse-square law). Doubling the distance cuts the force to one fourth.

cards.front: Ignoring air resistance, which falls faster: a bowling ball or a marble?
cards.back: Neither; all objects near Earth's surface fall with the same acceleration, g = 9.8 m/s², regardless of mass. Heavier objects feel more gravitational force, but they also need more force to accelerate, and the effects exactly cancel.

cards.front: What does the law of conservation of momentum say?
cards.back: In a closed system with no external forces, total momentum before an interaction equals total momentum after. It is why a cannon recoils backward when the cannonball flies forward.

cards.front: Why does a spinning skater speed up when she pulls her arms in?
cards.back: Angular momentum is conserved: it depends on rotation rate and on how far mass is from the spin axis. Pulling mass inward reduces that distance, so the rotation rate must increase to keep angular momentum constant.

cards.front: What force keeps an object moving in a circle, and where does it point?
cards.back: Centripetal force, which always points toward the center of the circle. For a car rounding a curve it is friction from the road; for the Moon it is Earth's gravity.

cards.front: Write the wave speed equation.
cards.back: v = fλ (speed = frequency x wavelength). 500 Hz x 0.68 m = 340 m/s, roughly the speed of sound in air.

cards.front: Write the equation relating a wave's period to its frequency.
cards.back: Frequency f is the number of wave cycles per second, in hertz (Hz); period T is the time for one cycle, in seconds. They are reciprocals: T = 1/f.

cards.front: What does a wave's amplitude tell you?
cards.back: How much energy the wave carries: larger amplitude means a louder sound or brighter light. Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the rest position, and it is independent of frequency and wavelength.

cards.front: Contrast transverse and longitudinal waves, with an example of each.
cards.back: Transverse: particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of travel, with crests and troughs (light, a shaken rope). Longitudinal: particles vibrate parallel to the travel direction, with compressions and rarefactions (sound).

cards.front: Why can light cross empty space while sound cannot?
cards.back: Sound is a mechanical wave that needs a medium of particles to compress; light is an electromagnetic wave of oscillating fields that travels through vacuum at 3 x 10⁸ m/s. That is why space is silent.

cards.front: List the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing frequency.
cards.back: Radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma ray. Frequency and energy increase along this order while wavelength decreases; within visible light, red is lowest frequency and violet highest.

cards.front: What is the difference between reflection and refraction?
cards.back: Reflection is a wave bouncing off a surface, like an echo or a mirror image. Refraction is a wave bending as it changes speed entering a new medium, like the apparent bend of a straw in water.

cards.front: What is diffraction? Give an everyday example.
cards.back: The bending and spreading of waves around obstacles or through openings. It is why you can hear someone talking around a corner; sound's long wavelengths diffract strongly around doorways.

cards.front: What happens in constructive versus destructive interference?
cards.back: Constructive: crests align with crests and amplitudes add, making a bigger wave. Destructive: crests align with troughs and amplitudes cancel; noise-canceling headphones use destructive interference.

cards.front: What happens to the observed frequency of a sound as its source approaches, then recedes?
cards.back: Approaching source: wavefronts are compressed, so observed frequency and pitch rise. Receding source: wavefronts are stretched, so pitch drops. This is the Doppler effect, heard as a passing siren's pitch falls.

cards.front: What evidence shows light behaves as both a wave and a particle?
cards.back: Interference and diffraction show wave behavior, while the photoelectric effect shows particle behavior: only photons above a threshold frequency eject electrons, no matter how bright the light. Light energy comes in packets called photons whose energy grows with frequency.

cards.front: State Ohm's law and solve: what current flows through a 4 Ω resistor connected to 12 V?
cards.back: V = IR, so I = V/R = 12 V / 4 Ω = 3 A. Current increases with voltage and decreases with resistance.

cards.front: Name the units for current, voltage, resistance, and electric power.
cards.back: Current: ampere (A). Voltage: volt (V). Resistance: ohm (Ω). Power: watt (W), with P = IV. A 120 V outlet driving 2 A delivers 240 W.

cards.front: Compare series and parallel circuits: current path and what happens when one bulb fails.
cards.back: Series: one path; a single burned-out bulb breaks the circuit and everything goes dark, and adding bulbs dims them all. Parallel: each device has its own branch at full voltage; one failure leaves the rest lit, which is why homes are wired in parallel.

cards.front: When a balloon is rubbed on hair, which particles move and what charges result?
cards.back: Only electrons transfer; protons stay locked in nuclei. The balloon gains electrons and becomes negative while the hair becomes positive, so they attract. Charge is transferred, never created or destroyed.

cards.front: Why do metals conduct electricity while rubber and plastic do not?
cards.back: Metals have loosely held outer electrons that move freely and carry charge. Insulators like rubber, plastic, and glass hold their electrons tightly, so charge cannot flow; that is why wires are copper with plastic coatings.

cards.front: What are magnetic domains, and which materials can be magnetized?
cards.back: Domains are microscopic regions where atomic magnetic fields point the same way; a material is magnetized when its domains align. Only ferromagnetic materials, chiefly iron, nickel, and cobalt, magnetize strongly; aluminum and copper are not attracted to magnets.

cards.front: Describe the field lines around a bar magnet, and what happens if you cut the magnet in half.
cards.back: Outside the magnet, field lines run from north pole to south pole and are densest at the poles, where the field is strongest; like poles repel, opposites attract. Cutting the magnet yields two smaller magnets, each with both poles; isolated poles do not exist.

cards.front: What is a solenoid, and what three changes make an electromagnet stronger?
cards.back: A solenoid is a coil of current-carrying wire that acts like a bar magnet. Strengthen it by adding more turns of wire, increasing the current, or inserting an iron core; reversing the current only flips the poles.

cards.front: How does a generator differ from a motor, and what principle does the generator use?
cards.back: A generator converts mechanical energy to electrical energy using electromagnetic induction: moving a coil relative to a magnetic field induces current, but only while the field through the coil is changing (Faraday's law). A motor is the reverse, converting electrical energy to motion.

cards.front: Write the formula for work.
cards.back: W = Fd: force times the distance moved in the direction of the force, measured in joules. If the object does not move, or the force is perpendicular to the motion, no work is done: holding a heavy box still does zero work on it.

cards.front: Write the formula for power.
cards.back: Power is the rate of doing work: P = W/t, measured in watts (1 W = 1 J/s). Two students lifting identical boxes do the same work, but the one who finishes faster develops more power.

cards.front: Write the formula for kinetic energy.
cards.back: KE = (1/2)mv^2, in joules. Because speed is squared, doubling speed quadruples the kinetic energy, and tripling speed makes it nine times greater.

cards.front: Write the formula for gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface.
cards.back: PE = mgh: mass (kg) times 9.8 m/s^2 times height (m), in joules. A 2 kg book lifted to a 1.5 m shelf stores about 29 J.

cards.front: Write Ohm's law as an equation.
cards.back: Ohm's law: V = IR, so volts = amperes x ohms. Rearranged as I = V/R, a 12 V battery across a 6 ohm resistor drives 2 A of current.

cards.front: Write the formula for electrical power in terms of current and voltage.
cards.back: P = IV, in watts; combined with Ohm's law it can also be written P = I^2 R or P = V^2 / R. A device drawing 5 A from a 120 V outlet uses 600 W.

cards.front: Write the efficiency formula as a ratio: what goes over what, before multiplying by 100 for percent?
cards.back: Efficiency = (useful output / total input) x 100. It is always below 100 percent because friction converts some input into waste heat: 400 J out for 500 J in is 80 percent efficient.

cards.front: Write the formula for mechanical advantage.
cards.back: MA = output force / input force; for an ideal inclined plane, MA = ramp length / ramp height. Machines multiply force but never energy: the smaller force is repaid by pushing through a longer distance.

cards.front: List the electromagnetic spectrum in order from longest wavelength to shortest.
cards.back: Radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma ray. As wavelength decreases along this list, frequency and photon energy both increase.
